Vignette: Mere

Mere is an eighty-year-old Māori woman who has spent the better part of six decades working with her hands. She learned to weld as a young woman in Auckland, one of very few women on the shop floor, and the work became a source of deep pride - the hiss of the torch, the smell of hot metal, the satisfaction of a clean, solid join. She still keeps her old welding mask on a shelf in her garage, though her hands are too unsteady now to do much more than hold it.

What happened to Mere did not happen once. It happened across the better part of a decade, during her first marriage in her late twenties and early thirties. Her first husband was charming in public and methodical in private. He hit her with his open hand, his closed fist, a leather belt, and once, a length of copper pipe. He told her it was her fault each time, and for a long while she believed him, because she had been taught that a good woman kept her home together. She left him eventually, after a night when she genuinely did not know if she would survive until morning. She packed one bag, took her two children, and drove to her sister's house in the dark.

She remarried in her forties - a gentle man, Tama, who has been her husband for nearly forty years. By most outward measures, Mere's life is full. She has grandchildren who visit on weekends, a garden she tends carefully, and a community at her local marae where she is respected and loved. She speaks of Tama with warmth and describes their marriage as the best thing that ever happened to her.

And yet. Mere has not slept through the night in years. She wakes in the early hours - three, four in the morning - her heart hammering, certain that someone is in the room. She lies still and listens, cataloguing sounds the way she once catalogued the sounds of her first husband's footsteps on the stairs. She knows it is Tama beside her. She knows she is safe. Her body does not seem to receive that information.

During the day, she is easily startled. A door slamming, a raised voice on the television, even the clatter of a dropped tool in the garage - any of these can send her heart into her throat and leave her shaking and short of breath for minutes afterward. She sometimes finds herself standing in the kitchen with no memory of how she got there, her mind having slipped somewhere she cannot quite name.

There are things she cannot watch. Any scene in a film where a man raises his hand toward a woman. She leaves the room. She does not explain why to her grandchildren.

What troubles Mere most, she says, is the shame that has outlasted everything else. She spent decades telling herself she was over it. She raised her children, built a life, loved a good man. She thought that was enough - that survival was the same as healing. Now, in her eighties, with her body slowing down and her nights growing longer, the memories come more insistently. She sees his face clearly. She remembers the particular weight of silence in the house before things turned bad, the way she learned to read the air like a pressure change before a storm.

She has told almost no one. She came to therapy, she says, because her youngest granddaughter - studying psychology at university - asked her once whether she had ever talked to anyone. The question stayed with her for two years before she made the call.

She sits with her hands folded in her lap, composed and dignified, and says she is not sure she deserves to take up space with something that happened so long ago. Then she looks out the window for a moment, and her face carries something that has clearly been carried for a very long time.
